chief_complaint: 5 days of high spiking fever unresponsive to antipyretics, bilateral conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, and rash (Kawasaki Disease)
hpi_details: 3-year-old boy brought to pediatric clinic with a 5-day history of high spiking fevers (up to 40.2C / 104.4F) that do not resolve with acetaminophen or ibuprofen. Over the past 3 days, mother noticed his eyes became bright red without pus, his lips turned dry, cracked, and bleeding, his tongue became bumpy and bright red like a strawberry, and a blotchy red rash appeared over his trunk and diaper area. Today noticed swelling and redness of the palms of his hands and soles of his feet.
ideas: mother exhausted and worried that 5 days of high fever is causing permanent damage
concerns: mother terrified by peeling red lips and bright bloodshot eyes without pus
expectations: wants specialized blood tests and immediate treatment to stop the fever and prevent heart damage

investigation_events.title: Urgent Kawasaki disease laboratory assessment
investigation_events.availability_message: The urgent inflammatory and supportive laboratory results are now available. Do not delay indicated IVIG while awaiting further testing.

results.value: 16-20 WBC/HPF with no bacteria, leukocyte esterase, or nitrites

investigation_events.title: Baseline transthoracic echocardiogram
investigation_events.availability_message: The baseline echocardiogram result is now available. A normal initial study does not exclude Kawasaki disease or remove the need for scheduled follow-up imaging.

results.value: Normal biventricular function; no coronary aneurysm, with maximal proximal coronary artery Z-score +1.8

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Kawasaki disease (complete/classic) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Admit to pediatric inpatient unit, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: 5 days of high spiking fever unresponsive to antipyretics, bilateral conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, and rash (Kawasaki Disease)

Key HPI features: 3-year-old boy brought to pediatric clinic with a 5-day history of high spiking fevers (up to 40.2C / 104.4F) that do not resolve with acetaminophen or ibuprofen. Over the past 3 days, mother noticed his eyes became bright red without pus, his lips turned dry, cracked, and bleeding, his tongue became bumpy and bright red like a strawberry, and a blotchy red rash appeared over his trunk and diaper area. Today noticed swelling and redness of the palms of his hands and soles of his feet.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 142, BP 94/60, Temp 39.9C. Physical exam reveals: 1. Bilateral non-exudative bulbar conjunctival injection with limbal sparing. 2. Oral mucocutaneous changes: erythematous cracked bleeding lips and prominent hypertrophic papillae forming a 'Strawberry Tongue'. 3. Polymorphous erythematous maculopapular rash across trunk and accentuated in the groin/diaper area. 4. Extremity changes: brawny edema and intense erythema of palms and soles. 5. Cervical lymphadenopathy: single firm, tender right cervical lymph node measuring 1.8 cm diameter (>1.5 cm). Labs: WBC 18,500 /uL with neutrophilia, Platelets elevated at 580,000 /uL (thrombocytosis), ESR 78 mm/hr, CRP 9.4 mg/dL. Sterile pyuria (>15 WBC/HPF without bacteria) on urinalysis.
Relevant background/PMH: No prior medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Kawasaki disease (complete/classic).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Scarlet fever without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever >=5 days unresponsive to antipyretics.
management_principles: Administer STAT single high-dose Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG 2 grams/kg over 10-12 hours) PLUS high-dose oral Aspirin (80-100 mg/kg/day divided q6h for anti-inflammatory effect until afebrile for 48 hours, then drop to low-dose antiplatelet aspirin 3-5 mg/kg/day)

Perform baseline 2D Transthoracic Echocardiogram immediately upon admission to establish coronary artery Z-scores and screen for coronary artery dilation/aneurysm (repeating echo at 2 and 6 weeks post-treatment)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) Clinical Practice Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: 3-year-old male presenting with 5 days of high persistent fever and all five classic mucocutaneous diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki Disease.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 142, BP 94/60, Temp 39.9C. Physical exam reveals: 1. Bilateral non-exudative bulbar conjunctival injection with limbal sparing. 2. Oral mucocutaneous changes: erythematous cracked bleeding lips and prominent hypertrophic papillae forming a 'Strawberry Tongue'. 3. Polymorphous erythematous maculopapular rash across trunk and accentuated in the groin/diaper area. 4. Extremity changes: brawny edema and intense erythema of palms and soles. 5. Cervical lymphadenopathy: single firm, tender right cervical lymph node measuring 1.8 cm diameter (>1.5 cm). Labs: WBC 18,500 /uL with neutrophilia, Platelets elevated at 580,000 /uL (thrombocytosis), ESR 78 mm/hr, CRP 9.4 mg/dL. Sterile pyuria (>15 WBC/HPF without bacteria) on urinalysis.
reference_soap.assessment: Complete (Classic) Kawasaki Disease (Mucocutaneous Lymph Node Syndrome) with high risk of Coronary Artery Aneurysm.
reference_soap.plan: Admit to pediatric inpatient unit. Administer STAT single high-dose Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG 2 grams/kg over 10-12 hours) PLUS high-dose oral Aspirin (80-100 mg/kg/day divided q6h for anti-inflammatory effect until afebrile for 48 hours, then drop to low-dose antiplatelet aspirin 3-5 mg/kg/day). Perform baseline 2D Transthoracic Echocardiogram immediately upon admission to establish coronary artery Z-scores and screen for coronary artery dilation/aneurysm (repeating echo at 2 and 6 weeks post-treatment). Critical guideline: IVIG must be infused within the first 10 days of illness onset to reduce coronary artery aneurysm risk from 25% down to <5%.

learning_objectives: Memorize the diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki Disease: fever >= 5 days plus at least 4 of 5 mucocutaneous features (conjunctivitis, oral/lip changes, rash, extremity changes, cervical lymphadenopathy >1.5 cm)
Explain the critical rationale and strict 10-day therapeutic window for high-dose Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG 2g/kg) combined with Aspirin to prevent permanent coronary artery aneurysms
Understand the unique exception allowing high-dose Aspirin in a febrile child (balancing Reye syndrome risk against coronary thrombosis/vasculitis prevention)
Schedule serial echocardiographic surveillance (baseline, 2 weeks, and 6-8 weeks) to track coronary artery Z-scores and detect aneurysms

teaching.one_liner: 3-year-old boy with 5 days of high fever unresponsive to antipyretics, conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, rash, and extremity swelling.

must_ask.objective: Confirm the fever duration and response to medication
must_ask.say: How many days has the fever lasted, and does it come down with medicine?

must_ask.objective: Ask about eye redness without discharge
must_ask.say: Are his eyes red but without any pus or discharge?

must_ask.objective: Ask about mouth and lip changes
must_ask.say: Have his lips become cracked or dry, and does his tongue look bumpy and red?
Have you noticed swelling or redness on his palms or the soles of his feet?

must_ask.objective: Explain the urgency of IVIG treatment
must_ask.say: We need to admit him today for a special IV medication and aspirin to protect his heart's blood vessels.

history.answer: My son has had a high fever for five days now, and it just will not go down even with medicine.
The fever started five days ago on Saturday morning, and it has stayed high the whole time.
It spiked up as high as 40.2 degrees, and it comes back in waves day and night with shivering.
I gave him children's Tylenol and ibuprofen around the clock, but his temperature barely drops.
No, he has not had any cough, runny nose, or trouble breathing at all.
He has not cried when peeing, and his diaper does not smell foul or look cloudy.
He has had no vomiting, stomach aches, or diarrhea, although his appetite is quite poor.
He seems cranky, but he recognizes me, moves his neck easily, and has not passed out.
A blotchy red rash started three days ago on his chest and belly, especially around his diaper area.
No, he has not had drenching night sweats or noticeable weight loss before getting sick.
I felt a firm, tender lump on the right side of his neck about two days ago.
We have not traveled anywhere recently, spent time in the woods, or touched stray animals.
None of the children in his preschool or anyone at home has been sick with a fever.
No, he has never had chemotherapy, steroids, or any immune-suppressing treatments.
He has never had any heart murmurs or defects, and he has not had any dental work done.
No, he was not taking any prescription medications before this fever began.
He is only three years old, so neither of those applies to him.
He is much more sluggish and irritable than usual, but he drinks some water and has not had seizures.
His eyes turned bloodshot three days ago, but there has been no yellow pus or crusting.
His lips became very red, cracked, and bleeding, and his tongue looks bumpy and bright red like a strawberry.
Just this morning, I noticed the palms of his hands and soles of his feet became swollen and bright red.
I am exhausted and terrified that five straight days of such high fever might cause permanent damage to his body.
I want proper blood tests and whatever medicine is needed right away to stop this fever and protect his heart.
He has always been a healthy boy with no prior illnesses or chronic conditions.
He has never had surgery, and this is the first time he might need to be hospitalized.
Only the children's acetaminophen liquid every four hours, which has not helped.
He has no known allergies to medicines, foods, or anything else.
No one in our family has autoimmune diseases, childhood heart problems, or recurrent fevers.
He lives at home with my husband and me, and attends a local preschool three days a week.
Neither my husband nor I smoke, and no one smokes around him.
He was born at full term through a normal delivery with no complications in the nursery.
His growth and development have always been right on track according to his pediatrician.
All of his routine childhood vaccinations are completely up to date.
His preschool reported no outbreaks of hand-foot-mouth disease, strep, or other illnesses.

exam.finding: Temperature is 39.9 C, blood pressure 94/60 mmHg, heart rate 142 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Irritable, flushed young boy resting in his mother's arms, appearing uncomfortable but consolable.
Bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without discharge or pus, with clear limbal sparing around the irises.
Both tympanic membranes are clear, translucent, and pearly gray with normal light reflexes.
Dry, cracked, bleeding red lips and diffuse pharyngeal erythema with prominent raised papillae showing a classic strawberry tongue.
A single firm, tender right anterior cervical lymph node measuring about 1.8 cm in diameter, without fluctuance.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with normal S1 and S2, without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Clear breath sounds throughout both lung fields with symmetric air entry and no wheezing or crackles.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender with no palpable masses or hepatosplenomegaly.
Brawny edema and striking redness on the palms of both hands and soles of both feet.
Polymorphous erythematous maculopapular rash spreading over the trunk and accentuated in the diaper area, without vesicles or petechiae.
Supple neck with full passive flexion, and negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
